## Quick Answer

**Question:** What's the best Korean cleanser for my skin type, and how do I know if the one I'm using is wrong?

**Answer:** The best Korean cleanser is a water-based second cleanse with a low pH (around 5 to 6) and a gentle surfactant matched to your skin type: a milk or cream cleanser for dry skin, a low-pH gel or foam for oily, something balanced for combination, and a fragrance-free low-pH formula for sensitive. If your skin feels tight, squeaky, or stings after washing, or if you're oilier by midday, your cleanser is too harsh and it's working against you.

---

## The Situation You're In

You rinse, you towel off, and your face feels... Clean. Tight-clean. That squeaky, just-washed-a-dish feeling that everyone told you means it worked. Then by 2pm your T-zone is an oil slick, or your cheeks sting when you put your serum on, or a new little bump shows up along your jaw that wasn't there yesterday.

Here's a thing you can do right now before you read another word: go grab your current cleanser and read the first five ingredients. If one of the first two is Sodium Lauryl Sulfate or Sodium Laureth Sulfate, or if you see fragrance (listed as "Fragrance" or "Parfum") high up, that's already a clue about why your skin feels the way it does. You don't need Korean to read that part. If you want the full breakdown of any ingredient on the list, the [Seoul Sister ingredient encyclopedia](https://www.seoulsister.com/ingredients) has individual pages for most of them.

This post is about the second cleanse, the water-based step. If you wear sunscreen or makeup, you oil cleanse first, and we covered that separately. This is the one that actually touches your bare skin every single night.

---

## Why This Happens

Most cleansers are built to feel dramatic, not to be kind to your barrier. That squeaky-clean sensation isn't cleanliness, it's your skin stripped of the oils and lipids it needs to hold water. When you strip those lipids, two things happen: your skin loses moisture and tightens up, and your oil glands often overcompensate by pumping out more sebum. That's the midday grease you're fighting. You're not oily because you're not cleaning enough. You might be oily because you're cleaning too hard.

The two things that actually separate a gentle cleanser from a harsh one are pH and surfactant type, and almost no marketing copy mentions either. Healthy skin sits around pH 4.7 to 5.5, slightly acidic, which is what keeps your barrier intact and your skin microbiome happy. A lot of traditional foaming cleansers run alkaline, up around pH 9 or 10, because that's what makes them foam aggressively. Washing at that pH disrupts your acid mantle and takes hours to recover from. A low-pH cleanser (roughly 5 to 6) cleans without that disruption. This is a big part of why so many Korean cleansers specifically advertise their pH. It genuinely matters.

Surfactants are the molecules that lift away oil and grime. Harsh ones like SLS clean effectively but strip indiscriminately. Gentler ones, amino-acid-based surfactants like sodium cocoyl glycinate or sodium stearoyl glutamate, clean well while leaving your barrier mostly alone. The name on the front of the bottle won't tell you which you're getting. The ingredient list will. That's the whole reason I pick these from the full INCI and not from the product name, because "gentle" on the front means nothing if sulfates are the second ingredient.

---

## What Actually Works

The honest answer is that "best" depends entirely on your skin type, so here's one water-based pick per type, each chosen from its actual ingredient list in the Seoul Sister catalog. If you want to browse more options across all of these, the full [cleanser category page](https://www.seoulsister.com/best/cleansers) has them sorted.

**Dry skin: a milk cleanser that cleans with oils, not just water.** For dry skin, you want a cleanser that removes the day without dragging your lipids out with it. The [ma:nyo Pure Soybean Cleansing Milk](https://www.seoulsister.com/products) is a milk-texture cleanser built around soybean extract, and milk cleansers in general are good for dry and mature skin because they lean on emollients rather than aggressive foaming. It holds a 5 out of 5 rating on Olive Young. One honest note: I haven't read this one's full INCI line by line here, so if fragrance is a dealbreaker for you, check the full list on the product page before you commit.

**Oily and combination skin: a low-pH gel or foam, but gently.** For oily and combo skin, the move is a low-pH water-based cleanser that controls oil without triggering the overproduction cycle I described above. This is also the one place a lightly foaming gel makes sense, because combo skin can handle a bit more cleansing in the T-zone. I'm not going to name a specific gel here that I haven't verified the ingredients on, because naming a plausible-sounding product from memory is exactly how people end up with a cleanser that's harsher than the one they're replacing. If your skin is oily, sensitive, and acne-prone all at once, that combination has its own rules and we broke it down in [the oily, sensitive, acne-prone cleanser post](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/best-cleanser-for-oily-sensitive-acne-prone-skin), which is a better read for you than this general one.

**Sensitive skin: low pH, soothing actives, and no surprises.** For sensitive skin, the [Etude SoonJung pH 5.6 Cleansing Milk](https://www.seoulsister.com/products) is the one I'd point to, and I can say that with confidence because I've read its full ingredient list. It's built on glycerin, caprylic/capric triglyceride, and sunflower seed oil for gentle cleansing, with panthenol for soothing and sodium stearoyl glutamate as a mild amino-acid surfactant. The pH is right there in the name at 5.6, which is exactly where you want to be. That lineup is about as low-drama as a cleanser gets.

**Barely-there sensitive or reactive days: a no-rinse micellar option.** On days when even a gentle milk feels like too much, or when you want a second cleanse without running water, [Bioderma Sensibio H2O](https://www.seoulsister.com/products) is a micellar water that lifts grime and makeup without rinsing. It's not Korean, but it earns its spot in a lot of sensitive-skin routines and it holds a 5 out of 5 on Olive Young. The brand describes it as fragrance-free; I'd still skim the full list on the product page if you react to anything specific, since I haven't read every line of it here.

One thing to notice across all of these: not one of them is picked because it foams the most or feels the most "deep clean." Cleansing is the step where doing less protects you. If your current routine keeps making your skin worse no matter what you add, the cleanser is one of the first places I'd look, and [this post on why skincare backfires](https://www.seoulsister.com/blog/why-does-my-skincare-keep-making-my-skin-worse) goes deeper on that.

If you've read all this and you're still not sure which type you actually are, or whether your current cleanser is the thing breaking you out, that's the kind of specific, your-routine question Yuri is built for. ---

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the best Korean cleanser for each skin type?

The best Korean cleanser for each skin type is a water-based second cleanse matched to what your skin actually needs:

- **Dry skin:** a milk cleanser like ma:nyo Pure Soybean Cleansing Milk that cleans with emollients instead of aggressive foam.
- **Oily and combination skin:** a low-pH gel or lightly foaming cleanser that controls oil without stripping and triggering more of it.
- **Sensitive skin:** Etude SoonJung pH 5.6 Cleansing Milk, built on glycerin, panthenol, and a mild amino-acid surfactant at a skin-friendly pH.
- **Reactive or no-rinse days:** Bioderma Sensibio H2O micellar water, which cleanses without rinsing.

### How do I know if my cleanser is too harsh?

Your cleanser is too harsh if your skin feels tight, squeaky, or stings right after you rinse, or if you're noticeably oilier by midday than you used to be. Those are signs it's stripping your barrier lipids, which both dehydrates your skin and pushes your oil glands to overproduce, so the "clean" feeling is actually a warning, not a win.

### Is a low-pH cleanser really better, or is that just marketing?

Low-pH cleansers are genuinely better for most people, not just marketing. Healthy skin is slightly acidic around pH 4.7 to 5.5, and washing with a cleanser at that same range (roughly 5 to 6) cleans effectively without disrupting your acid mantle, which highly alkaline foaming cleansers do. The pH is one of the few cleanser specs worth actively looking for.

### What's the difference between the best Korean face wash and the best Korean facial cleanser?

There's no real difference. "Korean face wash" and "Korean facial cleanser" are just different phrasings for the same water-based cleansing step, and both usually refer to the second cleanse that touches your bare skin after you've removed sunscreen or makeup with an oil cleanser. What matters is the formula, pH and surfactant type, not which of those names a brand prints on the front.

---

## The Bottom Line

The best Korean cleanser isn't the one that foams the hardest or leaves you squeaky. It's the gentlest one that still gets your skin clean, matched to your type, with a low pH and a mild surfactant you confirmed by reading the actual ingredient list instead of the front label. If your skin is tight after washing or oilier by midday, that's your sign the current one is working against you, and it's often the quietest reason a whole routine underperforms.

Start by reading your current cleanser's first five ingredients, then compare against a pick built for your skin type. If you want more options sorted and filtered, the [cleanser category page](https://www.seoulsister.com/best/cleansers) is the place to browse, and if you're genuinely stuck on which type you are, that's worth a conversation rather than another guess.
